The problem:
fluent text from no speech
  • Many audio segments (silence, music, environmental sounds, background noise) contain no speech, so the correct transcript is empty
  • A reliable ASR system transcribes speech accurately and stays empty when there is none
  • Whisper (Radford et al., 2023) is a state-of-the-art, widely used foundation model for ASR and robust speech processing
  • Its generative sequence-to-sequence decoder can emit fluent text even when the input contains no speech
  • For non-speech audio, any generated text is a hallucination
  • Outputs look plausible (acknowledgments, subtitle-style endings, conversational fillers, repeated fragments), so downstream systems may treat them as real speech
Research question: can non-speech hallucinations be reduced by editing Whisper's decoder activations at inference time?
01 · Introduction to the problem
3
Background:
how Whisper works
  • Transformer encoder–decoder trained on 680K hours of weakly supervised multilingual, multitask audio; strong zero-shot performance across languages, domains and acoustic conditions
  • Encoder maps audio to acoustic representations; the auto-regressive decoder generates text conditioned on the audio and previous tokens
  • Transcription and no-speech estimation share the same decoder: there is no separately trained speech activity detector
  • The decoder gives a probability to the special no-speech token <|nospeech|>, reported as no_speech_prob (pₙₛ in this deck)
  • Rejection heuristic: if pₙₛ exceeds threshold τ (default 0.6), the segment is rejected as non-speech
  • Failure mode: decoding is generative, so the model can still give high probability to fluent token sequences when acoustic evidence is weak or absent
02 · The problem in depth
4
Existing mitigations:
where each one acts
Input · VAD
WhisperX (Bain et al., 2023) removes non-speech regions before decoding
Limit: needs an external segmentation model
Model · fine-tuning
Calm-Whisper (Wang et al., 2025) trains hallucination-related decoder parts on non-speech audio with empty transcripts
Limit: extra training; may overfit to its data
Decoding · heuristics
Thresholds on no-speech probability, log probability, compression ratio (Radford et al., 2023)
Limit: act only on output-level scores
Output · filtering
Bag of Hallucinations (Barański et al., 2025) removes known phrases after decoding
Limit: misses unseen hallucinations; can remove valid speech
Gap: none of these edit decoder activations at inference time. Hidden-state interventions already reduce hallucinations in LLMs and vision-language models (Yang et al., 2025; Dastmalchi et al., 2026).
02 · The problem in depth
5
Proposed solution:
gated low-rank decoder projection
Training-free, at inference time: no parameter updates, no external VAD, no phrase lists. Key idea: hallucination-prone non-speech behaviour lives in a low-rank subspace of decoder hidden states that can be projected away.
01
Calibrate
Collect decoder hidden states for non-speech clips that hallucinate vs. clips correctly left empty
02
Estimate
SVD of their differences gives the top-r directions: the hallucination subspace, then kept fixed
03
Project
At one decoder layer, remove each hidden state's component along that subspace (strength α)
04
Gate
Apply it only when Whisper's own no-speech probability is at least γ
  • Two variants: always-on (projection on every input) and gated (only when Whisper predicts likely non-speech)
  • Why the decoder: it both generates text and provides the no-speech evidence, so the method acts before tokens are emitted
03 · Proposed solution
6
Step 1:
calibration activations
Let ℓ be a decoder layer and d its hidden-state dimension. A non-speech calibration set gives two groups of layer-ℓ decoder hidden states:
Hℓ = { hᵢ,ₗʰᵃˡˡ }, i = 1 … N_h Fℓ = { hⱼ,ₗᵉᵐᵖᵗʸ }, j = 1 … N_f hᵢ,ₗʰᵃˡˡ , hⱼ,ₗᵉᵐᵖᵗʸ ∈ ℝᵈ
  • Hℓ: non-speech inputs where Whisper produces a non-empty, hallucinated transcript (N_h examples)
  • Fℓ: non-speech inputs correctly rejected, with no transcript (N_f examples)
  • Estimated only from the calibration set (ESC-50 folds 1–3), then kept fixed
04 · The solution in depth
7
Step 2:
low-rank subspace estimation
Both groups are non-speech, so differencing cancels shared acoustic factors and keeps the hallucination-related behaviour.
1 · Difference matrix, with n = min(N_h, N_f):
Δℓ ∈ ℝⁿˣᵈ, row i = ( hᵢ,ₗʰᵃˡˡ − hᵢ,ₗᵉᵐᵖᵗʸ )ᵀ
2 · SVD: the right singular vectors with the largest singular values are the dominant directions where the groups differ
Δℓ = Uℓ Σℓ Vℓᵀ
3 · Keep the top r as a row-orthonormal projection basis; rank r sets the dimension of the removed subspace
Bℓ,r = Vℓ,1:rᵀ ∈ ℝʳˣᵈ
04 · The solution in depth
8
Step 3:
inference-time decoder projection
A forward hook at the selected decoder layer replaces each hidden state hℓ ∈ ℝᵈ:
h̃ℓ = hℓ − α ( hℓ Bℓ,rᵀ ) Bℓ,r   (1)
hℓ Bℓ,rᵀ
coordinates of hℓ along the r hallucination directions
( hℓ Bℓ,rᵀ ) Bℓ,r
the component of hℓ inside the hallucination subspace
α
projection strength; with orthonormal rows, α = 1 removes the component fully, smaller α removes part of it
  • Intuition: remove the directions that make non-speech inputs produce text, and keep the information normal transcription needs
  • No change to model parameters or to the decoding procedure
04 · The solution in depth
9
Step 4:
no-speech-conditioned gating
  • Eq. (1) on every input can perturb real speech, so it is applied only when Whisper's own no-speech estimate is high
  • pₙₛᵇᵃˢᵉ = no-speech probability from a first, unprojected pass; γ = gate threshold
h′ℓ = hℓ − α ( hℓ Bℓ,rᵀ ) Bℓ,r  if pₙₛᵇᵃˢᵉ ≥ γ h′ℓ = hℓ  if pₙₛᵇᵃˢᵉ < γ
  • Gate open: decode again with the projection; otherwise keep the unprojected output
  • The resulting pₙₛ is then compared with τ for the final rejection decision
γ decides WHEN the activation intervention is applied
τ decides WHETHER the segment is rejected (default 0.6)
04 · The solution in depth
10
Evaluation:
metrics and parameters
HR
Hallucination rate: non-speech inputs whose output is still non-empty after no-speech filtering (reference is empty)
WER
Word error rate on LibriSpeech, the cost to real transcription
FRR
False rejection rate: fraction of speech samples wrongly rejected by the no-speech filter
Four parameters, one forward hook on one decoder layer
ℓ
decoder layer
r
rank of the subspace
α
projection strength
γ
gate threshold
Whisper's default no-speech threshold τ = 0.6 throughout. Parameters are chosen per Whisper scale (different depth and hidden size), once, on ESC-50 folds 1–3 plus LibriSpeech validation-clean (only to control speech degradation), then fixed for every held-out evaluation.

05 · Results
13
What it means:
the hallucination results
01
Hallucination is low-rank. A fixed subspace of 1 to 4 directions at one decoder layer pushes non-speech inputs over the rejection threshold.
02
It transfers across datasets. Calibrated on ESC-50 folds 1–3 and tested on folds 4–5, UrbanSound8K and FSD50K, which suggests a reusable decoder-level signature, not ESC-50-specific acoustics.
03
Depth matters most, rank saturates. Early layers are weak, middle-to-late layers strong; more directions are not better and can remove speech-relevant information.
04
The baseline problem is severe. Original large-v3 hallucinates on 76.08% of UrbanSound8K clips: 0.87% always-on, 2.74% gated.
05
Always-on vs. gated. Always-on gives the lowest HR; gated is slightly higher on large-v3 (8.38% vs 1.50% on ESC-50) but protects speech. For small they are nearly identical (1.53% vs 1.50%).
06 · Interpreting the results
14
Our contributions:
reproduce, then test it
Setup
  • Whisper small, fp16, on an RTX 3050 6 GB laptop GPU; about 3 hours end to end
  • Greedy decoding, English forced, 30 s window; reject when pₙₛ > τ = 0.6
  • Seeded test subsets: 800 ESC-50, 2,000 UrbanSound8K, 2,000 FSD50K, 1,000 + 1,000 LibriSpeech
Four contributions
  1. Reproduction on Whisper small, including the paper's own operating point
  2. Threshold baseline the paper omits: τ chosen on dev by the paper's own rule, compared clip by clip
  3. Analysis of what the gate and the edit do, and why the last layer fails
  4. Affine variant: move states to the empty-class mean instead of zero
07 · Our contributions
15
Why the last layer fails:
and our affine fix
Paper, Eq. (1): project to zero
h̃ = h − α (h Bᵀ) B
At layer 12, clips with pₙₛ > 0.6 drop from 78.7% to 0% at every rank: nothing is rejected, so HR is 100%
Ours, Eq. (2): move to the empty-class mean
h̃ = h − α ((h − c) Bᵀ) B
c = mean of the F states at layer ℓ. Clips with pₙₛ > 0.6 rise from 78.7% to 95.2% (r = 1) and 99.4% (r = 8)

08 · Results of our contributions
19
Affine variant:
keeps speech, misses new sounds
  • Keeps speech: FRR 0.35% and WER 5.68%, against 1.35% and 6.58% for Eq. (1)
  • Generalises poorly: held-out HR 12.61% against 4.0% on dev; FSD50K sound classes are not in ESC-50
  • Still loses to a threshold: at equal HR (τ = 0.46) it rejects 7 utterances, the threshold 0 (p = 0.016)
Why it breaks at other settings
c is the mean at the SOT position, but the hook edits every position. At ℓ11 r8 the decoder emits only “<|zh|><|zh|>…”: WER 99.6% on edited utterances
A side effect we do not count
Always-on affine lowers test-clean WER 3.31 → 2.92 (−0.39 [−0.77, −0.09]) but not test-other (+0.24 [−0.17, 0.69])
08 · Results of our contributions
20
What this means:
issues in the paper's evaluation
1
The key control is missing. The τ sweep stops at 0.5, though the paper's own medium ablation shows plain HR 29.49% → 13.08% from τ 0.6 to 0.4
2
At the published small setting the edit adds nothing on speech: every gated utterance is rejected
3
WER mixes two errors. On accepted utterances the edit does no harm; the whole cost is rejecting short utterances
4
Projecting to zero is not neutral. An affine target fixes the last layer, but one SOT centre at every position breaks decoding
5
Labels come from pₙₛ, so the subspace partly re-learns the no-speech read-out, consistent with unchanged AUROC
6
Tuning ignores noisy speech: our Eq. (1) setting had 0% FRR on dev-clean but 2.5–3.3% on test-other
7
Internal inconsistencies: validation WER 3.94% vs 11.59%, medium α 0.75 vs 1.0, FSD50K 21.35% for two models, the FSD50K count
Limits of our study: Whisper small only, one seed, held-out subsets, no WhisperX VAD run
08 · Results of our contributions
21
In summary:
seven things to remember
Problem
Whisper hallucinates fluent text on non-speech audio (large-v3: non-empty on 44.25% of ESC-50 and 76.08% of UrbanSound8K clips)
Method
Training-free, low-rank decoder activation projection, calibrated once on non-speech data and fixed, optionally gated on Whisper's own no-speech probability
Results
Average HR 31.31% → 2.44% (always-on) and 3.74% (gated): relative reductions of 92.21% and 88.05%
Cost
Gated WER +0.33 to +4.39 points and FRR 0.41% to 9.97%; the HR–WER–FRR trade-off is controllable through τ, γ and α
Vs. baselines
Large-v3 gated average HR 4.09% beats WhisperX VAD (5.24%), BoH (44.09%) and threshold tuning (45.99%), with no external detector, phrase list or fine-tuning
Our reproduction
On Whisper small the paper's HR reproduces (3.14% vs 3.07%), but plain Whisper with τ = 0.17 chosen on dev does at least as well (HR 0.87%, WER 5.93%, same FRR); at equal HR every projection rejects more speech
Our affine variant
Moving states to the empty-class mean fixes the last-layer failure and nearly removes false rejections, but it generalises poorly (held-out HR 12.61%)
